articles.title: Sales of tinned food and bottled water  jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.summary: Sales of essential goods such as hand sanitiser soar after the government called on households to be prepared for emergencies.
articles.content:
Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.

Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".

The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a government campaign successfully encouraging households to prepare for emergencies by stocking essential supplies. This has a positive real-world impact by increasing community resilience to severe weather or cyberattacks, with broad significance for the general public. The article provides detailed context on the campaign's effects and consumer behavior, showing a meaningful, measured response rather than panic buying.
articles.personality_title: Government campaign boosts sales of emergency supplies without panic buying
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The government launched a campaign called "Be Ready" on October 22 to encourage people to prepare for emergencies like severe weather or cyberattacks. They asked households to keep enough food, water, and other essentials to last for three days.

**What happened** – In the 10 days after the campaign started, sales of important items rose significantly. Hand sanitiser sales increased by 83%, bottled water by 67%, and canned or jarred food by 37%. Data showed that an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, but most bought normal amounts, showing they were gradually stocking up.

**Impact** – This shows that many people listened to the government’s advice and started preparing without panic buying or hoarding. Instead of rushing to buy large amounts, more households simply added recommended items to their regular shopping. This response helps communities be better ready for emergencies.

**What's next step** – The government and companies like food producer Princes will continue to monitor how people prepare. The campaign may encourage more people to keep emergency supplies at home and help businesses plan for future demand.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After the "Be Ready" campaign, more households are calmly stocking up on emergency essentials, improving preparedness without causing shortages.
articles.personality_title_fr: La campagne gouvernementale stimule les ventes de fournitures d'urgence sans achats paniques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le gouvernement a lancé la campagne "Soyez prêts" le 22 octobre pour encourager les gens à se préparer aux urgences comme les intempéries ou les cyberattaques. Il a demandé aux foyers de garder assez de nourriture, d'eau et d'autres essentiels pour trois jours.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Dans les 10 jours suivant le début de la campagne, les ventes d'articles importants ont beaucoup augmenté. Les ventes de gel désinfectant ont augmenté de 83 %, celles d'eau en bouteille de 67 % et les aliments en conserve ou en bocaux de 37 %. Les données montrent que 400 000 personnes supplémentaires par jour ont acheté de la viande en conserve, mais la plupart ont acheté des quantités normales, ce qui montre qu'elles se préparaient progressivement.

**Impact** – Cela montre que beaucoup de gens ont suivi les conseils du gouvernement et ont commencé à se préparer sans paniquer ou faire des réserves excessives. Au lieu de se précipiter pour acheter en grande quantité, plus de foyers ont simplement ajouté les articles recommandés à leurs courses habituelles. Cette réponse aide les communautés à mieux se préparer aux urgences.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement et des entreprises comme le producteur alimentaire Princes continueront de suivre la préparation des gens. La campagne pourrait encourager plus de personnes à garder des fournitures d'urgence chez elles et aider les entreprises à planifier la demande future.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après la campagne "Soyez prêts", plus de foyers font calmement des provisions d'essentiels d'urgence, améliorant leur préparation sans provoquer de pénuries.
articles.personality_title_es: La campaña del gobierno impulsa ventas de suministros de emergencia sin compras de pánico
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El gobierno lanzó la campaña "Prepárate" el 22 de octubre para animar a las personas a estar listas para emergencias como el mal tiempo o ciberataques. Pidieron a los hogares que guardaran suficiente comida, agua y otros esenciales para tres días.

**Qué pasó** – En los 10 días después del inicio de la campaña, las ventas de artículos importantes aumentaron mucho. Las ventas de gel antibacterial subieron un 83 %, las de agua embotellada un 67 % y las de alimentos enlatados o en frascos un 37 %. Los datos mostraron que 400,000 personas adicionales por día compraron carne enlatada, pero la mayoría compró cantidades normales, lo que indica que se estaban abasteciendo poco a poco.

**Impacto** – Esto muestra que muchas personas siguieron el consejo del gobierno y comenzaron a prepararse sin comprar de forma impulsiva o acaparar. En lugar de apresurarse a comprar grandes cantidades, más hogares añadieron los artículos recomendados a sus compras habituales. Esta respuesta ayuda a que las comunidades estén mejor preparadas para emergencias.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno y empresas como el productor de alimentos Princes seguirán observando cómo se preparan las personas. La campaña puede motivar a más personas a tener suministros de emergencia en casa y ayudar a las empresas a planificar la demanda futura.

**Resumen en una frase** – Tras la campaña "Prepárate", más hogares están almacenando con calma suministros esenciales para emergencias, mejorando la preparación sin causar escasez.

articles.title: Prehistoric Britons may have made giant stone axes to show off
articles.summary: Unusually large handaxes weighing up to 3 kilograms have puzzled archaeologists because they are so unwieldy, but their function may have been purely symbolic
articles.content:
Unusually large handaxes weighing up to 3 kilograms have puzzled archaeologists because they are so unwieldy, but their function may have been purely symbolic

Examples of giant handaxes found in Britain, measuring 253 millimetres and 285mm long Courtesy of the British Museum and The Seaside Museum, Herne Bay

More than 300,000 years ago, hominins in Britain were crafting huge, skilfully shaped handaxes whose primary purpose may have been for showing off.

Giant ficrons, weighing up to 3 kilograms and measuring up to 30 centimetres long, were fragile and impractical to wield – but tricky and time-consuming to knap. Accomplished stone tool-makers thus probably fashioned these rare knives not for cutting but as a sort of prehistoric status symbol, says Malaika Standley Barrow at University College London.

“These giant ficrons really are lovely, and it seems they’re meant to visually stand out and be appreciable to other group members as something unusual and interesting to look at,” she says. “So there’s definitely some prowess or something – or maybe a creation of social bonds through the act of doing this together.”

Advertisement

Ficrons are Stone Age handaxes carved from flint with curved sides, rounded bases and remarkably pointed tips. Named for the sharp iron tips of poles once used to propel French boats through shallow water, these tools have appeared in archaeological records in Britain since the late 19th century, particularly along the Thames and its tributaries.

Most ficrons are similar in size to other handaxes from this period, measuring about 8 to 15 centimetres long, and probably worked as cutting or butchering knives. But a few stand-out ficrons exceed two or even three times the usual length and 10 times the weight – and scientists don’t know what purpose they might have served.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Our Human Story Sign up to newsletter

To address that question, Standley Barrow and her colleagues examined 817 ficrons and other handaxes from seven archaeological sites across southern Britain, stretching across the Thames valley, Kent, Hampshire and Devon. Among those tools were seven giant ficrons measuring at least 22 centimetres long.

3D scans and measurements revealed that six of the seven giant ficrons had extremely exaggerated proportions compared with smaller handaxes from the same sites. The giant handaxes also tended to be more symmetrical and have straighter edges than smaller versions, suggesting they were crafted with more skill and precision. This means these larger axes weren’t simply scaled-up versions of standard ficrons, but probably deliberately crafted to be visually distinct, says Standley Barrow.

The researchers then commissioned experienced flintknappers to make 10 giant and 10 normal-sized replica ficrons from British flint. Next, they had 20 students use the replicas to cut through 10 pieces of rope attached to metal frames. Each student completed the task first with an ordinary-sized ficron, followed by a giant one.

Knappers like James Dilley at Ancient Craft in Norfolk, UK, found the giant ficrons particularly challenging to make, especially the fine tip. “You have to think of the flint as being very much like a piece of glass,” he says. “One misplaced strike and it will snap in half, and all that work has gone to waste. You need a lot more skill and experience to make one of these.” On average, knapping a giant ficron took about 45 minutes, compared with about 20 to 30 for smaller ficrons, he says.

Yet there seemed to be no practical benefits for this extra work: on average, the students took 22 per cent more time cutting the rope with giant ficrons, often resorting to using two hands to manoeuvre a heavy knife they found difficult to control. For butchering or digging, pressure on the blade would probably break the tip quite easily, Standley Barrow adds.

Even so, it’s possible the blade could have been used both ceremoniously and practically for delivering a killing blow to a wounded prey, known as the coup de grâce, she and her colleagues argue.

Luke Dale at Durham University, UK, finds that concept particularly compelling. The giant ficrons could have had limited practical use in a culturally important role and hold a prominent social function, he says.

The age of the tools suggests they were probably made by early Neanderthals. The exquisite craftsmanship of these objects points to an interest in aesthetics and cultural tradition, adding to the evidence that our ancient ancestors were more sophisticated than people often consider them to be.

“These were clearly intelligent archaic humans who could use technology to survive, and presumably had very recognisable social interactions with each other,” says Dale.

Journal Reference: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports DOI: 10.1016/j.jasrep.2026.106120
articles.reasoning: The article reveals a significant archaeological discovery about prehistoric Britons crafting giant stone axes likely as social status symbols, highlighting early human cultural sophistication and social behavior. This insight into human history has broad educational and cultural value, inspiring curiosity about our ancestors and their social practices.
articles.personality_title: Prehistoric giant stone axes in Britain were likely made to show off
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Over 300,000 years ago, early humans in Britain made stone tools called handaxes. Most were practical tools for cutting, but some were much larger and heavier, puzzling archaeologists because they seemed hard to use.

**What happened** – Researchers studied 817 handaxes from southern Britain, including seven giant ones up to 30 centimeters long and weighing 3 kilograms. They found these giant axes were carefully and skillfully made, more symmetrical and precise than smaller ones. Experts made replicas and tested them cutting rope, showing the big axes were harder to use and less practical.

**Impact** – The study suggests these giant handaxes were not made for everyday work but as symbols to show skill and status in early human groups. This reveals that early Neanderthals had an interest in art, social bonds, and cultural traditions much earlier than previously thought.

**What's next step** – Scientists will likely continue studying these tools and other artifacts to learn more about early human behavior and social life. This could change how we understand the intelligence and culture of our ancient ancestors.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Giant stone axes made by prehistoric Britons were likely crafted as special symbols to display skill and social status, showing early humans valued culture and craftsmanship.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les axes en pierre géants préhistoriques en Grande-Bretagne servaient probablement à impressionner
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a plus de 300 000 ans, les premiers humains en Grande-Bretagne fabriquaient des outils en pierre appelés haches à main. La plupart étaient pratiques pour couper, mais certaines étaient beaucoup plus grandes et lourdes, ce qui a intrigué les archéologues car elles semblaient difficiles à utiliser.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs ont étudié 817 haches à main dans le sud de la Grande-Bretagne, dont sept géantes mesurant jusqu’à 30 centimètres et pesant 3 kilogrammes. Ils ont découvert que ces grandes haches étaient fabriquées avec beaucoup de soin, plus symétriques et précises que les plus petites. Des experts ont fabriqué des répliques et les ont testées pour couper de la corde, montrant que ces grandes haches étaient plus difficiles à utiliser et moins pratiques.

**Impact** – L'étude suggère que ces grandes haches n’étaient pas faites pour un usage quotidien, mais comme des symboles pour montrer l’habileté et le statut social dans les groupes humains anciens. Cela montre que les Néandertaliens avaient un intérêt pour l’art, les liens sociaux et les traditions culturelles bien plus tôt qu'on ne le pensait.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques vont probablement continuer à étudier ces outils et d’autres objets pour mieux comprendre le comportement et la vie sociale des premiers humains. Cela pourrait changer notre vision de l’intelligence et de la culture de nos ancêtres.

**En une phrase** – Les axes en pierre géants fabriqués par les Britons préhistoriques étaient probablement des symboles spéciaux pour montrer l’habileté et le statut social, révélant que les premiers humains valorisaient la culture et le savoir-faire.
articles.personality_title_es: Las hachas de piedra gigantes prehistóricas en Gran Bretaña probablemente se hicieron para impresionar
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hace más de 300,000 años, los primeros humanos en Gran Bretaña fabricaban herramientas de piedra llamadas hachas de mano. La mayoría eran prácticas para cortar, pero algunas eran mucho más grandes y pesadas, lo que desconcertaba a los arqueólogos porque parecían difíciles de usar.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores estudiaron 817 hachas de mano en el sur de Gran Bretaña, incluyendo siete gigantes de hasta 30 centímetros de largo y 3 kilogramos de peso. Encontraron que estas hachas grandes estaban hechas con mucho cuidado, eran más simétricas y precisas que las más pequeñas. Expertos hicieron réplicas y las probaron cortando cuerda, mostrando que las hachas grandes eran más difíciles de usar y menos prácticas.

**Impacto** – El estudio sugiere que estas hachas gigantes no se fabricaron para el trabajo diario, sino como símbolos para mostrar habilidad y estatus social en los grupos humanos antiguos. Esto revela que los neandertales tenían interés en el arte, los lazos sociales y las tradiciones culturales mucho antes de lo que se pensaba.

**Próximo paso** – Es probable que los científicos sigan estudiando estas herramientas y otros objetos para aprender más sobre el comportamiento y la vida social de los primeros humanos. Esto podría cambiar cómo entendemos la inteligencia y cultura de nuestros antepasados.

**Una frase clave** – Las hachas de piedra gigantes hechas por los britones prehistóricos probablemente eran símbolos especiales para mostrar habilidad y estatus social, demostrando que los primeros humanos valoraban la cultura y la artesanía.
